articles.title: Two cities, two road projects, one problem: Mumbai redesigns Ghatkopar bridge as Delhi struggles with Barapullah
articles.summary: Mumbai and Delhi are asking the same uncomfortable question from either end of two big road projects: did planners consider how people would actually use
articles.body: Mumbai and Delhi are asking the same uncomfortable question from either end of two big road projects: did planners consider how people would actually use the roads? After the work on Mumbai’s Ghatkopar road overbridge is almost 30% complete, it is being redesigned. In Delhi, Barapullah Phase-III opened with a promise of a 15-minute journey but within days of opening, it is facing serious congestion. One project is being changed before it’s finished and another is being redone after commuters began using it.The Ghatkopar redesign is significant as it involves changing a structure that is already under construction. Three pier caps – RP15, RP16 and RP17 – will need partial demolition and rebuilding at a higher level. The original plan had a 2+2-lane cable stayed bridge as the main east-west connection. Instead, the revised plan creates a two-tier setup, separating local traffic between Ghatkopar East and West from longer-distance traffic between the Andheri side and the Eastern Express Highway.Mumbai’s lessonThe logic behind the Mumbai redesign is simple. A resident travelling from Ghatkopar East to West to attend school, visit a market, hospital, railway station or ward office should not have to mingle with traffic passing through the area. Nor should residents have to take a longer detour simply because the main bridge is designed primarily for vehicles travelling across the area. The proposed lower-level road overbridge between Shreyas (LBS) Junction and Pant Nagar Junction is meant to address just this problem of local movement.The main bridge will be raised a few meters and widened to a 3+3-lane configuration to accommodate heavier volumes of through-traffic. It is an acknowledgment that a road corridor can have two very different types of user: those passing through the city and those making short, everyday trips in their own neighborhood. The Mumbai Traffic Police says it has to deal with over 2.7 million vehicles across the city every day, while Ghatkopar itself has had to impose temporary one-way restrictions recently due to heavy movement of vehicles on local roads.Delhi’s lessonBarapullah Phase-III presents the problem from the other side. The 3.5-km-long elevated corridor is planned as a major connectivity project connecting Mayur Vihar Phase-I with Sarai Kale Khan. The bigger Barapullah network is expected to provide a largely signal-free route to South Delhi. Official estimates have said that journeys toward AIIMS could be reduced from around 35-40 minutes to around 15 minutes. Instead, tailback of almost 3km was reported shortly after opening, with commuters reporting journeys of 40 minutes or more.The problem appears to be not just the amount of road space available, but what happens when different streams of traffic converge. A joint inspection by Delhi Traffic Police and PWD, with the help of drone footage, found the merger point near Sundial Park as a major bottleneck where traffic from the multiple-lane elevated corridor merges into a narrower existing section, with vehicles from other directions also joining the same stretch. The result is a classic urban traffic problem. Capacity at one point, but an unresolved conflict at the next.The awkward question in both the citiesThe striking similarity between Ghatkopar and Barapullah is that the problem is not whether a bridge or an elevated road is needed. Both are real traffic needs. The bigger question is whether road planning is keeping up with the complexity of urban movement. Mumbai has opted to alter the Ghatkopar design before its completion, necessitating demolition and additional work to prevent an expected clash between local and through traffic. Now Delhi is trying to manage a conflict that only came into view after thousands of motorists entered the corridor.The Barapullah experience has also shown another modern problem – navigation technology can make a road-design problem worse. Delhi Traffic Police said Google Maps was not showing the congestion and kept directing motorists to the corridor. The police finally asked commuters to use NH-24 and the DND Flyway. Possible short-term measures being considered include an additional lane, a dedicated U-turn and changes to traffic management at the merger.There’s a bigger lesson here for India’s fast growing metros. Mumbai's new Ghatkopar bridge is being planned for an 80 to 100-year horizon while Delhi's Barapullah project was expected to change the way people move between East and South Delhi. But infrastructure for long-life cannot be measured by how many lanes it has or how fast a vehicle can travel on a stretch. It has to explain where those vehicles are coming from, where they are joining, where they are turning, and why local inhabitants use the road differently than passing commuters.Hence the difference between the two cities matters. Mumbai is spending more time and energy now to change a bridge before the traffic starts flowing. Delhi is finding out that a road built to save time can also become a bottleneck at its most crucial intersection as traffic has begun to move. In both cases, the real test of infrastructure is not the opening, the length of the bridge or the number of lanes. articles.title: One missed email, a wrong turn: How China got hold of sensitive US F-35 stealth fighter parts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A warning email was apparently lost in the machinery of a global logistics chain, and what followed was an embarrassing detour involving some
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A warning email was apparently lost in the machinery of a global logistics chain, and what followed was an embarrassing detour involving some of the most sensitive components of America’s F-35 stealth fighter.A United Parcel Service Inc. employee apparently missed an email instructing that a shipment containing F-35 parts must not pass through certain countries. The shipment was subsequently routed through Hong Kong, potentially putting sensitive US military technology within China’s reach, according to a person briefed on the incident who spoke to Bloomberg.The fresh details, reported by Bloomberg on Wednesday, offer a new explanation for how the F-35 components ended up being diverted through Hong Kong. The missing parts were first reported by Bloomberg last month, but the newly revealed email lapse has shed further light on how a series of logistical errors may have allowed the shipment to reach a route that US regulations specifically sought to prevent.The email that was missedThe shipment included an F-35 cockpit canopy and a weapons-bay door, both coated with radar-absorbing material designed to enhance the aircraft’s stealth characteristics.The parts were being returned to the US in late May for possible repair or disposal, according to people familiar with the incident. They were originally supposed to travel to San Francisco through South Korea and Taiwan, both US defence partners.But after the shipment left Australia later than expected, it was mistakenly routed through Hong Kong in an effort to speed up delivery, the person told Bloomberg.Before that happened, freight forwarder DSV A/S had sent an email warning that the shipment carried an International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR, designation and could not transit through certain countries. The regulations are designed in part to prevent sensitive US military technology from reaching adversaries.DSV was handling the shipment on behalf of F-35 developer Lockheed Martin Corp. The person familiar with the incident said the email may have been sent through a different IT system from the one used by the UPS employee who handled the shipment.The previously unreported details were presented by Pentagon officials during a roughly hour-long briefing on September 29 with staff members of the House foreign affairs and armed services committees.Why the F-35 parts matterThe episode has raised concerns in Washington because the F-35 is not just another military aircraft. It is the world’s most advanced fighter jet and the most expensive weapons programme in US history. China has also spent years targeting the aircraft through espionage efforts.Both components were covered with radar-absorbing material, which contributes to the aircraft’s ability to evade detection.Diana Maurer, who oversees F-35 support reviews at the non-partisan Government Accountability Office, told Bloomberg that the loss of the components was a serious concern.“It’s not good the Chinese now have” an F-35 canopy, she said, calling the loss “a big deal.”“I’m sure the Chinese celebrated and then they got busy trying to reverse engineer it and figure out how to counter it with their own technical capabilities,” she added. “I’m sure that’s what they were up once they got those things.”The incident has triggered investigations by the Pentagon and State Department and prompted US lawmakers to demand a wider review of the global supply chain used to move American military equipment.Pentagon faces questions over supply chainThe Pentagon has sought to distance itself from responsibility for the errant shipment while stressing that the parts were “unserviceable”.The US Transportation Command said it “was not involved in the transportation or coordination of the shipment in question.”The Department of Defense said it was working to recover the components and investigate what happened.“We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the Defense Department said in a statement.At the September 29 briefing, Erica Plath, the deputy assistant secretary of defense for logistics, said a team she had assembled was taking steps to prevent a similar incident from happening again, according to the person familiar with the meeting.A State Department compliance official from the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls, which enforces US defence export controls, also attended the briefing. The directorate is investigating the diversion.The episode has also drawn scrutiny from Capitol Hill. Senator Mark Warner, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, had demanded the Pentagon briefing, while committee chairman Senator Tom Cotton called for a review of the military supply chain.Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, who chairs the Armed Services Committee panel investigating the incident, has also questioned whether the diversion was accidental.“Did China have a plan all along to intercept this?” Cramer asked.Lockheed, UPS decline to commentLockheed Martin, which manages much of the global spare-parts pool supporting F-35 operations for the US and 19 other countries, said last month, when Bloomberg first reported the missing components, that “our logistics decisions are not made unilaterally.”The company said it selects carriers based on their ability to comply with government regulations.“While we cannot discuss the details of which logistics partner was involved, we are working closely with them to help develop and implement preventive measures to strengthen our collective oversight and prevent recurrence,” Lockheed said.After being presented with the newly reported details about the diversion, Lockheed said on Wednesday that “we have nothing to add or correct on the series of events you mentioned.”DSV spokesman Stephan Ghisler-Solvang and UPS spokesman Malcolm Berkley declined to comment.The incident has nevertheless exposed a potentially serious vulnerability in the movement of sensitive military hardware: even when export restrictions are clearly laid out, a missed email and a hurried logistical decision can send highly sensitive components down a route they were never supposed to take.

articles.title: America’s debt crisis threatens our children’s future. We the People need to fix it
articles.summary: America's national debt has surpassed $40 trillion, burdening every citizen with roughly $117,000 in debt as interest costs reach $1 trillion a year.
articles.body: If your house were on fire and your children were inside, you would not shrug and say that you are only one person and therefore powerless. You would run toward danger because the people you love were at risk and because waiting would be an act of surrender. America is facing a different kind of fire. It is a fiscal fire, and our children and grandchildren are already inside the house. Some have heard warnings about the national debt for so long that they conclude nothing terrible ever happens. Others believe a single voice cannot possibly matter. Some do not think the problem is serious. Others assume that because the United States remains the world’s strongest economy, nothing can bring us down. Those habits of mind ignore how different this moment is from anything we have faced before. The national debt has now surpassed $40 trillion, a sum so large it is almost impossible to hold in the mind and a burden of roughly $117,000 for every man, woman and child in the country. The size of the number is daunting, but the direction of the path is what should keep us awake. WASHINGTON IS DRIVING AMERICA TOWARD A DEBT CRISIS WE CAN'T IGNORE ANY LONGER The federal government continues to spend more than it collects, and deficits stretch into the multi-trillion-dollar range year after year with no end in sight. Social Security and Medicare carry unfunded obligations measured in the tens of trillions, and there is no serious plan to close the gap. The trust funds will be exhausted in a few years, and current law would then force major benefit cuts. Interest costs already exceed $1 trillion a year and consume more than one fifth of total federal revenue, and that share is growing. The Government Accountability Office says the federal government is on an unsustainable fiscal path that poses serious economic, national security and societal challenges. These are not partisan talking points. They are mathematical realities, and they make today unlike any earlier chapter in our history. MEDICARE IS ONE OF AMERICA’S GREATEST SUCCESSES — AND A FISCAL TIME BOMB At some point, debt stops being an abstract figure in a government report and becomes a direct threat to the economy. Investors will eventually lose confidence and stop buying our debt at rates we can bear. That is when the Ponzi structure collapses and a fiscal crisis arrives. We cannot wait for that day, as if surprise will make the outcome more honorable. America’s greatest economic strength has always been its people, the men and women who work, save, invest, build businesses, raise families and solve hard problems. We inherited an extraordinary country from previous generations. We have a moral obligation to leave our children and grandchildren a country at least as strong as the one we received, not one that is bankrupt. $50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT There is no painless way out of a problem this large. Getting government spending and deficits under control will mean restraint, entitlement reform, stronger growth and choices that some voters will dislike. Those choices still must be made while there is time, because the pain of discipline now is small next to the wreckage of a failed financial system, when savings shrink, credit dries up, businesses fail and even basic government promises will be harder to guarantee. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The answer ultimately rests with "We the People." Congress will not fix the problem because economists produce another report or one president gives another speech or because one political party suddenly discovers fiscal virtue. It will happen when the American people understand how serious the danger is and demand that Congress repair the mess it has created. That is the power of our voices and our votes. One citizen will not change Washington. Millions of individual decisions can become a political force that Congress cannot ignore. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Our house is on fire. Once we recognize and accept that reality, we will act. The remaining question is whether we will act before the damage becomes irreversible. Our children and grandchildren are counting on us. We should not leave them in a burning house. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM LES RUBIN

articles.title: UK police charge Royal Navy member accused of working with foreign power
articles.summary: Police say the incident is not connected to ongoing investigations at the RAF Fairford airbase.
articles.body:
Police in the United Kingdom say they have arrested and charged a member of the Royal Navy accused of working with an unnamed foreign power after an investigation by counterterrorism police.

Teddy Young, 24, was charged with two offences under the National Security Act for allegedly obtaining protected information and preparing to transfer it for the benefit of a foreign power.

In a statement, authorities alleged that between November 2024 and May 2025, Young “obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power… contrary to section 1 of the National Security Act 2023″.

Young is due to appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court later on Thursday.

“These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces,” Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement.

“We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter,” she added.

UK media reported that the officer was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday before he was taken into custody in London.

The police clarified that the case is not related to the ongoing investigation into an incident at the RAF Fairford airbase .

articles.title: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature
articles.summary: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson who combines the classical and the modern won the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday.
articles.body: STOCKHOLM — Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature Thursday for playful, genre-blending works that fuse the classical and the modern. Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often mix elements of poetry, essay and fiction. Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said Carson was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the academy reached her to notify her of the win. “She was very taken by surprise,” Carlberg said. Works range from classical Greek translations to poetry Carson’s books include “Eros the Bittersweet,” a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel “Autobiography of Red,” “Men in the Off Hours,” a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy. She also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the Swedish Academy said, “may be regarded as independent works in their own right.” They include “If Not, Winter,” based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles’ tragic plays “Electra” and “Antigone” and Euripides’ “Bakkhai.” “Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the literature committee. Olsson added that Carson’s juxtaposition of influences ranging from the ancient Greeks to John Keats, Virginia Woolf and Emily Bronte “leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.” Carson wrote about her own life and struggles Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022. She also has drawn on her own life for works such as “Nox,” which was published in 2010 and dealt with the decades-long absence and then death of her brother Michael. Olsson called it “a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother.” It also includes Carson’s translation of an elegy by the Roman poet Catullus for his own brother. Among her most recent work is, “Wrong Norma,” a 2024 a wide-ranging collection of pieces from publications including The Paris Review and The New Yorker, accompanied by Carson’s hand-drawn illustrations. Also that year, Carson wrote in the London Review of Books about being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. She said “a symptom particularly mortifying to me was that my handwriting disintegrated. “Hard to describe or explain the shame of bad handwriting,” she said. “Bad handwriting is ugly. Also it is inauthentic. In the sense it is not you.” The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. The Associated Press’ efforts to reach Carson and her literary agent, Nicole Aragi, were not immediately successful. Friday to bring peace prize winner The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million) per prize. Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humor, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.” Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs. This week ends with Friday’s peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

articles.title: Indian actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar dies at 75
articles.summary: Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker, died Thursday at his home in the western state of Goa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI — Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker, died Thursday at his home in the western state of Goa. He was 75. Patekar died of a suspected cardiac arrest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported, citing a doctor at the hospital where he was pronounced dead. Born in 1951 in India’s western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built a career spanning nearly five decades in Hindi- and Marathi-language cinema. He was known for intense performances and roles that often portrayed complex or unconventional characters. Patekar made his film debut in the 1978 Hindi film “Gaman,” and later earned acclaim for “Parinda” and “Krantiveer.” Patekar became popular in mainstream Bollywood films, while also working in India’s “parallel cinema” movement, known for its focus on realism and social issues. He gained wider international recognition with filmmaker Mira Nair’s Oscar-nominated “Salaam Bombay!” He won three National Film Awards, India’s highest film honors, and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honors. In 2018, during India’s #MeToo movement, a Bollywood actress accused Patekar of sexual harassment on a film set. Patekar denied the allegation. The case was among several that drew attention as women publicly spoke about sexual misconduct in India’s film industry. Prime Minister Narendra Modi mourned Patekar’s death, praising his “intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence” as an actor. “He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations,” Modi wrote on X. Patekar is survived by his wife and son.

articles.title: Celebrity chef says military lesson is key to keeping families together
articles.summary: One in six military families faces food insecurity. Robert Irvine and USAA's Fuel to Serve initiative aims to change that, starting at the dinner table.
articles.body: Some of the most important conversations do not begin in an office or a classroom — they begin around the dinner table, celebrity chef Robert Irvine said. "Food is hope, is love, is community, communication and caring," Irvine told Fox News Digital in an interview from his home in Florida. "When we sit across from the table with each other, we can see what's going on." That belief is behind Fuel to Serve, a new five-year partnership between the United Services Automobile Association (USAA) and the Robert Irvine Foundation, designed to use food and shared meals as a starting point for supporting military families. DOCTORS IN TRAINING LEARN COOKING SKILLS TO HELP PATIENTS AMID AMERICA'S CHRONIC DISEASE CRISIS The initiative, announced at the end of September, will begin with pilots at Fort Bragg and in the Washington, D.C., region. It aims to connect service members and their families with cooking and nutritional education, financial resources, mental health support, benefits navigation and community programs. Irvine, founder and chairman of the Robert Irvine Foundation, said the partnership expands his longtime effort to improve military food systems and help families build practical skills at home. The partnership is allowing Irvine to go "wider and broader and deeper," he said. "I think we have the ability to bring people back together again over a family table," he said. 'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS In addition to his longtime work supporting service members, veterans and military families, Irvine is a restaurateur and television personality known for hosting Food Network's "Restaurant: Impossible." Around his family's dinner table, it's "phones down," he said. "We communicate, and that's what I've got going on with the military right now, which is amazing to see," he added. "Why not plan your food?" The chef said the work is about more than getting a healthier meal on a plate. It also involves helping families understand food labels, planning meals, shopping on a budget and preparing dinner quickly after a long day. RFK JR TAKES MAHA TO THE KITCHEN WITH HHS COOKING SERIES PROMOTING HEALTHY MEALS FOR UNDER $5 For families trying to cook nutritious meals on a budget, Irvine recommends making a weekly menu and grocery list, then spending time prepping ingredients in advance. "Planning is essential in everything we do," he said. "Why not plan your food?" FREE TOOL HELPS FAMILIES SAVE MONEY BY USING FOOD ALREADY IN THEIR KITCHENS He said basic preparation — such as chopping an onion, boiling eggs or putting together ingredients on a quieter day — can make it easier to get a meal on the table in about 20 minutes. "Food is the entry point, the front door." For military families, the stakes can be especially high, and the Robert Irvine Foundation says one in six military families faces food insecurity. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Lindsey O'Neill, who leads communications and public affairs for USAA, pointed to research from the Military Family Advisory Network that found more than 41% of military-affiliated respondents experienced low or very low food security — a figure that rose to 57% among junior enlisted respondents. Separately, Blue Star Families found that 30% of active-duty families said they often or sometimes could not afford balanced meals, according to O'Neill. Frequent military moves can add another challenge and force families to rebuild their support systems every few years, O'Neill said. "What better way than the dining table, the dinner table and food to create that natural entry point," O'Neill said. articles.title: Three sisters who drowned in sea off Brighton took own lives, inquest finds
articles.summary: Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters, who lived in London, drowned in the sea in May.
articles.body:
Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled.

Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, had been living "very secluded lives" following the death of their mother, who drowned in 2010, senior coroner Penelope Schofield said.

On 11 May, the women - who had all been living together in Greenford, London - visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died before travelling the next day to Brighton beach, where they drowned in adverse sea conditions in the early hours of 13 May. The coroner said they could not swim.

Their father Joseph Jacobsen said it was heartbreaking to lose "all three of my precious daughters".

He was among family members who followed proceedings via video link.

In an emotional statement read out on his behalf, he said he watched his daughters grow from little girls to beautiful, intelligent women "with a special place in my heart".

He said: "There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child.

"To lose all three of my precious daughters is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined."

He could not understand why his daughters' lives ended so suddenly, and hoped they were reunited with their mother "in God's eternal care", he added.

If you are experiencing emotional stress, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line here.

The coroner told the court: "These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private, we don't know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton.

"It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known."

The hearing was told the sisters left their home in London and arrived in Brighton together by taxi at 22:21 BST on 12 May.

The Uber driver had noted the lack of conversation during their journey.

The three appeared to pace the seafront in the darkness, with CCTV sightings of them at different points along Brighton's east beach. They were last seen alive at 02:42 on 13 May.

Police searched Christina's laptop and found 227 references to water and 179 references to suicide.

The coroner said Christina had been experiencing anxiety and depression since the death of her mother.

Rebecca's medical records showed "nothing of note" and Jane was not registered with a doctor, Det Ch Insp Mark Cullimore told the court.

A previous inquest into their mother's death had found her cause of death was drowning.

Postmortem tests revealed toxicology results for all three sisters were negative for drugs and alcohol. There was no evidence to suggest they had been subject to violence.

Ms Adetoro was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene on the morning of May 13, the inquest heard.

Christina Walters, who worked in accountancy, was recovered from the sea by an RNLI lifeboat, and Rebecca Walters, who worked in HR, was washed on to the shore of Brighton beach. They were also pronounced dead that morning by paramedics.

articles.title: Eritrean troops cross into northern Ethiopia as conflict escalates
articles.summary: Eritrean soldiers entered two towns in northern Ethiopia, a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government said, with military officers conducting surveillance in one of them, as residents reported that Tigrayan opposition forces had withdrawn from the city of Shire.
articles.body: Eritrean soldiers entered two towns in northern Ethiopia, a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government said, with military officers conducting surveillance in one of them, as residents reported that Tigrayan opposition forces had withdrawn from the city of Shire. Ermiyas Ababu, a Tigray Peace Force commander based in Mekelle, said Eritrean personnel entered Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday. He said Eritrean military officers and commanders were conducting surveillance in Idaga Hamus, citing reports from his personnel in the area. Separately, conflict monitoring group ACLED said Eritrean troops crossed the border at Zelambesa on Wednesday and Ethiopian military drones targeted them at Guada as they traveled toward Idaga Hamus. The Associated Press could not independently verify either account. ACLED, which provided its account through East Africa analyst Jalale Getachew Birru, had not responded Thursday morning to an inquiry about the basis for its claims. The allegations come amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and an opposition alliance that includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF. Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Wednesday of fabricating allegations to justify military action against his country. In a post on X, he accused Ethiopia’s ruling party of creating “a fallacious narrative of ‘self-defense.”’ He did not specifically address the movements or strikes described by ACLED. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated Monday that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that it remained committed to dialogue and peaceful engagement with its neighbors. Eritrea has denied Ethiopia’s allegations that it supports the TPLF. Last week, it announced it was severing diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara. In Shire, residents Mesu’ud Ahmed and Abadi Halefom told the AP by telephone Wednesday evening that they had witnessed TPLF forces withdrawing earlier that day. Government troops and allied forces had not entered when they spoke, Mesu’ud said. Shire has been a major refuge for people displaced by fighting in Tigray and a base for humanitarian aid operations. “TPLF left but the government forces and their allies did not enter the town but we hear that they are coming,” Mesu’ud said. “Everyone has closed their shops in Shire, and moved their merchandise for fear of looting.” Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, on Sunday after the TPLF announced its withdrawal. The Tigray Peace Force imposed a curfew there Wednesday from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. The force includes former members of the TPLF’s armed wing. Ermiyas said Tuesday that it was working with Ethiopian federal troops to expand its control. The TPLF joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy. Fighting escalated late last month, undermining the November 2022 peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war.

articles.title: The Hormuz bonus: Sailor salaries soar for transits amid Iran war
articles.summary: Reports have emerged that tanker captains are earning $100,000 plus a $50,000 per-trip bonus to transit the strait.
articles.body:
As shipping traffic through the besieged Strait of Hormuz fell to its lowest level since July this week, reports have emerged that sailors are being paid large bonuses for making the dangerous trip through the Gulf waterway.

Some captains are earning base salaries of as much as $100,000 – the high end of usual salaries which vary greatly between shipping companies – plus a $50,000 bonus per voyage through the strait, the UK’s Financial Times has reported.

Oil exports from the Middle East rose above pre-war levels at the end of last month despite ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. But shipping data from Kpler shows that about 40 percent of those are leaving the region due to a combination of pipeline exports and small shuttle boats carrying out risky ship-to-ship transfers.

Are oil exports getting through the strait?

Yes. According to shipping data from Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels left the region last month, matching the pre-war average, excluding Iran, which is under a naval blockade by the United States.

However, about 40 percent of this is being exported via Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline or via ship-to-ship transfers by smaller boats travelling undetected through the strait.

Kpler reported on Tuesday that the number of detectable vessels passing through the strait had fallen to its lowest level in more than two months, with only seven vessels passing through the crucial waterway in the previous week, the lowest figure since July 23.

Data is hard to determine, as many smaller shuttle boats are turning off their transponders to avoid detection when travelling through the strait before offloading oil to larger tankers waiting beyond it.

How dangerous is it for sailors in the strait?

Very. Attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued in the past week.

On Wednesday night, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several casualties after multiple projectiles struck a vessel sailing off Qatar’s northern coast.

Following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February, Tehran all but closed the strait, with limited vessels receiving clearance. Iran has launched strikes at ships making the crossing without its express permission.

The US, for its part, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports due to Tehran’s closure and has escorted some vessels through the waterway.

Last week, attacks on tankers in the strait hit their highest level since the war began as regional oil producers tried to increase exports at heightened risk for crew and cargo.

Saul Kavonic, energy head at MST Marquee, told the Reuters news agency: “The frequency of Iranian attacks on ships is now at the highest point since the war began, and likely to intensify further.”

He added that “constrained product flows, extreme logistics costs and high likelihood of Iranian escalation are keeping [oil] prices elevated”.

Oil prices rose on Thursday morning, with Brent crude futures increasing by $2.28, or 2.28 percent, to $102.28 a barrel by 04:27 GMT.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained $1.66, or 1.88 percent, to $89.94.

This is despite oil exports recovering to some extent due to Saudi Arabia using alternative export infrastructure and due to the complex system of ship-to-ship transfers.

The East-West pipeline , which carries oil from fields in Saudi Arabia’s east to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, has been crucial to this process. However, it has also come under threat and been forced to close at times due to strikes from Iran-backed groups.

What incentives are sailors receiving for crossing the strait?

The Financial Times reported this week that tanker captains can now command a base salary of $100,000, plus a $50,000 per-trip bonus, to make the dangerous transit.

Overall, the crew on board each ship can earn four to six times their normal salaries.

On Monday, The Wall Street Journal reported that shipping companies were spending between $30m and $40m for a single round trip to move oil in and out of Hormuz through ship-to-ship transfers.

It added that oil producers now have to swallow high costs to get oil out of the waterway, with shipowners and individual sailors making some of the best returns the industry has seen in decades. Many sailors willing to risk the trip are coming from India, the Philippines and China to do so.

“One Shandong-based ship-staffing company is even offering as much as $25,000 for a round trip as reward, according to seafarers and recruitment advertisements seen by The Wall Street Journal. For oilers and cadets [low-level crewmembers of a commercial ship] the $25,000 could represent more than a year of wages,” the outlet reported.

As with the smaller shuttle boats that move in and out of the strait under threat of attack, captains on board larger ships and tankers must turn off their lights and transponders to make the journey.

According to Bloomberg, which spoke to a captain on a vessel that was part of the shuttle runs, his vessel, which frequently carries barrels at night, is given strict instructions: no lights, no phones, and only one radar on as they cross.

Speaking from the Philippines, where he has arrived following a three-month stint taking vessels through the strait, he explained that he and his crew got their bearings by using the coast and lighthouses as a reference, adding that it is “quite challenging”.

After seeing a fire ahead on one trip, the captain said he called the US Navy, which has been assisting ships on routes through the waterway to avoid mines, to warn them of an attack.

He added that his most recent contract through the strait was shorter than usual since he knew the voyage was “not easy”, but he still received several times his usual salary for the trip.

Another captain of a Liquefied Natural Gas tanker told Bloomberg that his journey began by turning off the breaker that connects the ship’s location transponder to hide their whereabouts while they were travelling along the Omani coast.

Crew members also barricade the main decks with sandbags in case drones or missiles attack them.

The report added that shipping executives estimate a one-in-20 chance of being hit while crossing the strait at present.

articles.title: Gaten Matarazzo swaps Stranger Things for Rent in West End
articles.summary: The actor opens up about finding his way in the West End as he makes his debut in a revival of Rent.
articles.body:
Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference.

You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience.

The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End.

He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous.

Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life".

The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next.

"It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo

"We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film."

"I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it."

Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in .

But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child.

He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds".

"My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says.

"Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time.

"I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane."

In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends.

It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now".

"What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says.

"That's really fun to sing in context of today."

When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis.

It was considered groundbreaking at the time for tackling social taboos and centering stories of LGBT people.

Writer Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its premiere.

Matarazzo's co-star, Travis Ross, who plays Roger, says the show's themes still "ring true" today.

The 25-year-old says having Rent tends to attract people who "care so deeply" about the show's message, resulting in a connection between actors and the audience.

He calls it a "really beautiful community-driven piece of art".

Both Ross and Matarazzo are keen to acknowledge their fellow cast members and point out Rent is "an ensemble" piece.

"In the same way we get our moments to tell the story there's also ten other people who get their moments to tell the story as well," says Ross.

Many of those in the audience will be there to watch Matarazzo, and he says he's determined to get the role right.

"I'm on stage for the majority of the show and singing the whole time," he says.

"It's not anything that's particularly high or out of my range, it's actually a part that I think fits nicely in my pocket.

"But it's just so much singing, and making sure I'm doing it correctly is essential," he says.

Matarazzo also plans to embrace his return to the stage.

"Once we're in the run it will be great," he says.

"I just always love the opportunity to start and finish a character arc and story in real time.

"You don't get an opportunity to do that when you're filming."

Speaking of which - if he ever got the call to go back to Hawkins and step into Dustin's shoes, would he take the chance?

"If that happens, that's great, and if not, that's completely fine.

"I've loved doing the show so much, it's literally the greatest honour of my life."

Rent is at The Tom Stoppard Theatre, London. Gaten Matarazzo is booked to perform until 10 January.

articles.title: Ex-councillor guilty of running sham Covid-19 testing lab
articles.summary: Faisal Shoukat is convicted of fraudulent trading and money laundering after a trial.
articles.body:
A former councillor has been found guilty of running a bogus coronavirus testing laboratory during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Faisal Shoukat, who served on Calderdale Council, was convicted of causing public nuisance, fraudulent trading and money laundering after a trial at Bradford Crown Court.

Four other people on trial alongside Shoukat, former justice minister Shahid Malik, Lynn Connell, Paul Moore and Dr Alexander Zarneh, were cleared of all charges.

The verdicts were returned by His Honour Judge Chris Smith after the jury was discharged in April during their deliberations, when one member of the panel was arrested on suspicion of conspiring to pervert the course of justice.

During the trial, prosecutors said 39-year-old Shoukat - who was a Labour councillor at the time - was the "controlling mind" of RT Diagnostics, based in Halifax.

The court heard that test kits sent out to customers - sourced from Turkey - did not meet the required standards in the UK.

It was also heard the lab had returned a "suspiciously low" number of positive tests .

Between May and July 2021 it reported 123,104 tests, but only 45 of these were positive, with 123,058 showing as negative and one indeterminate.

A video published by The Sun newspaper in July of that year alleged tests were being dumped in a side room.

The video also showed the firm's laboratory at Park Works to be in poor condition, with rubbish strewn across the floor, its ceiling exposed and bin bags dumped outside.

Medical safety inspectors described the site on Lister Lane as a "building site" and said there was evidence of people living there.

Delivering his verdicts, Judge Smith criticised the company's "cavalier" and "careless" approach to the accreditation process, which would allow it to conduct testing.

Shoukat, a pharmacist, told the trial he was paid around £1.5m in shares from the firm.

Mr Malik, who cried after he was cleared of wrongdoing, was also paid a similar amount as a co-director, the court heard.

He was not involved in the day-to-day running of the company, and lived outside of the UK for part of its short-lived tenure.

articles.title: Bear kills man in home attack near Mongolian capital
articles.summary: Police say the bear entered a traditional nomadic dwelling near Ulaanbaatar, killing a man and seriously injured a woman.
articles.body:
A bear has killed a man and seriously injured a woman after it attacked them in their home near the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar.

Police say the incident happened in the Bayanzurkh district overnight on Wednesday in their traditional Mongolian nomadic tent-like structure known as a ger.

The man, who was in his 40s, died, but the woman, in her 50s, managed to flee and raise the alarm with neighbours. She is in a serious condition in hospital, city official Munkhbayar M told reporters.

Sightings of bears around humans are becoming more common in Mongolia, for reasons that include climate change and food scarcity.

A team of rangers is searching for the bear while officials have warned locals to be vigilant and report any sightings.

There had been 24 bear sightings near the capital this year alone, compared to just two in 2018, Munkhbayar said, in comments reported by the AFP news agency.

Videos showing bears entering or damaging gers, and attacking livestock have reportedly gone viral on Mongolian social media in recent weeks, highlighting the increase in bear and human interaction across the country.

Bear-hunting permits across eight provinces have been issued and officials are seeking to obtain tranquiliser dart guns to support rangers in rural areas, AFP reports.

A significant amount of Mongolians are nomadic, but settled agricultural communities are becoming more common. An increasing number of the population lives in the capital or other major urban areas.

articles.title: The backstory: Che Guevara's final hours - 'You are only going to kill a man'
articles.summary: “I know you are here to kill me.
articles.body: “I know you are here to kill me. Shoot, you are only going to kill a man.”Nearly six decades after his death, Che Guevara is still 39 - and still on T-shirts.Like Marilyn Monroe, Kurt Cobain and Bob Marley, Che has remained frozen in time, forever young in the public imagination. The grey hair never came, the face never aged and he is always dressed for battle.With his beret and unruly hair, his image still appears on T-shirts, coffee mugs and protest banners, turning the Argentine-born revolutionary into an enduring symbol for generations of young rebels.The doctor who wanted to treat the worldErnesto Guevara de la Serna was born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1928. He studied medicine but was swept towards the dream of revolution. In 1951, he set out on a trip with his friend Alberto Granado on La Poderosa II around South America. His experience with poverty, sickness and exploitation - documented in The Motorcycle Diaries - turned a restless medical student into a committed Marxist.Along the way, he picked up the nickname "Che", which loosely translates to ‘yaar’ in Hindi.In 1954, he met Fidel Castro and became his most trusted field commander during the 1956-58 guerrilla war that overthrew Cuban dictator Fulgencio Batista.After the January 1959 victory, he held key posts in Castro's government. He became the head of the national bank and industry minister and helped push Cuba towards a Soviet-aligned, centrally planned system. He also became the leading theorist of foco warfare, the belief that a small, disciplined armed group could ignite a wider uprising.Cuba's declining economy, US sanctions and Che's radicalism brought him into conflict with the Cuban leadership. In 1965, he eventually resigned from the Cuban government and vanished from public view.From Cuba, he went to Congo to support the liberation movement founded by Patrice Lumumba. The effort, however, fizzled out and he landed in Bolivia in hopes of turning the country into the base of a continent-wide revolution.The Bolivian campaignGuevara arrived in Bolivia in November 1966, in disguise. He established the National Liberation Army of Bolivia with plans to win over peasants in the country and eventually challenge President René Barrientos.He had dreamed of bringing his version of revolution to the heartland of South America while he was fighting in the Sierra Maestra of Cuba a decade earlier."I’ve got a plan. If some day I have to carry the revolution to the continent (South America), I will set myself up in the forest at the frontier between Bolivia and Brazil. I know the spot pretty well because I was there as a doctor. From there it is possible to put pressure on three or four countries and, by taking advantage of the frontiers and the forests, you can work things so as never to be caught," Che had once written.However, the plan didn't work. By October 1967, Che Guevara’s Bolivian guerrilla campaign was collapsing. His small band was exhausted, short of food and increasingly isolated from local support.Meanwhile, the US CIA was closing in on the revolutionary following his disappearance from Havana.How Che was capturedOn October 8, Bolivian forces, trained and assisted by the United States, cornered the guerrillas near the village of La Higuera. Guevara was wounded in the fighting.He was shot in the leg and the rifle was knocked from his hands. Unable to continue, he surrendered.“Do not shoot! I am Che Guevara and worth more to you alive than dead,” he reportedly told the soldiers.The captured guerrilla leader was then taken to a one-room schoolhouse in La Higuera, where he was held overnight. The next day, CIA operative Félix Rodríguez, a Cuban American working with the Bolivian military, found Guevara inside.'I should have never been captured alive'Washington wanted Guevara kept alive for interrogation. But Bolivia’s military leaders decided that a public trial would turn him into an even greater revolutionary symbol. They ordered his execution and planned to claim that he had died in combat.In an interview many years after the incident, Rodríguez recalled telling Guevara that he was going to be killed.According to Rodríguez, the guerrilla leader accepted his fate and said, “It’s better this way. I should have never been captured alive.”He then instructed the soldier assigned to carry out the execution to shoot Guevara below the neck, so his death could be presented as the result of battlefield wounds.“I know you’ve come to kill me. Shoot, you are only going to kill a man,” Che told Sgt. Jaime Terán, the man tasked with killing him.The bullets struck Guevara in the arms, legs and thorax. The 39-year-old guerrilla leader died on October 9.Bolivian soldiers took his body to Vallegrande and laid it on a hospital laundry sink, where journalists and photographers were allowed to see and photograph him.Authorities also ordered his hands cut off so his fingerprints could be taken and used to establish his identity.Within days, news of his death reached Washington. A memorandum to US President Lyndon B Johnson concluded: “This removes any doubt that ‘Che’ Guevara is dead.”Fidel Castro later told a massive crowd in Havana that those who believed Guevara’s death had defeated his ideas were mistaken.“They are mistaken who believe that his death is the defeat of his ideas,” Castro said.Che returns to CubaThirty years later, a team of Cuban specialists and Argentine forensic experts located a mass grave beneath an airstrip in Vallegrande. The remains were exhumed and Che’s skeleton was identified along with those of several of his fallen comrades.In 1997, Che's remains were flown to Havana, where Fidel Castro presided over a televised ceremony at San Antonio de los Baños airbase. Che’s daughter handed the urns containing the remains to the Cuban state.The remains then lay in state at Havana’s Plaza de la Revolución before being taken to Santa Clara, the city where Che had helped secure a decisive victory during the 1958 Cuban Revolution.On October 17, Castro led the final burial at the newly built Che Guevara Mausoleum in Santa Clara. In a ceremony watched across Cuba, he made clear that the occasion was not meant to mark the end of Che’s story.“We have not come to say goodbye to Che,” Castro declared. “We have come to welcome him.”You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows
articles.summary: NHS winter pressures appear to be building already, with rises in waiting times for planned surgery.
articles.body:
There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders.

The warning comes as new data reveals the waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row.

An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

The numbers are the highest since October 2025 and have raised questions over whether the NHS will meet a government target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.

The rise in waiting lists comes despite the NHS in England delivering what were described as record levels of planned, elective care over the summer, while demand for services also reached its highest level ever.

A record 4.7 million planned treatments, procedures and appointments occurred across June, July and August – more than in any previous summer.

But both A&Es and ambulance services also saw a record number of patients for the month of September.

NHS England's national medical director, Professor Frankie Swords, warned that despite the progress delivered by frontline teams, winter pressure was already building.

"Staff are already seeing the ominous early signs of pressure, with more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year, and unfortunately many people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she said.

The NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, says the government in England is not going to achieve its manifesto promise of hitting the 18-week hospital waiting time target by the end of the parliament in 2029.

That 18-week target hasn't been hit for a decade.

A separate analysis by the Health Foundation think-tank said progress on cutting waiting times had stalled over the past year, with referrals on to the waiting list rising at a much quicker rate than the number of patients being treated.

Sir Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance which represents NHS trusts, said: "The NHS continues to respond to record demand for care, but the relentless growth in demand for services is putting NHS staff under real pressure."

Francesca Cavallaro, of the Health Foundation, said: "Thanks to the hard work of staff, the NHS has made progress in bringing down waiting times, but a rise in referrals mean that the service is having to run faster just to stand still and the prospects of meeting the government's pledge are receding.

"Andy Burnham's government have yet to set out whether they will give the 18-week target the same priority as it had under Keir Starmer, but our analysis shows the pledge is becoming increasingly hard to deliver."

"Not just numbers, but vulnerable people"

There will be concern too that the pressures of a long, hot summer have merged almost seamlessly into the pressures associated with the winter months.

More patients, including children, have been arriving at A&E departments with flu and other respiratory viruses.

The number of patients seen within four hours in A&Es last month fell to 74.4%, down from 75.0% in August.

The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted – what is known as "corridor care" – stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.

That has alarmed Dr Vicky Price, president of the Society for Acute Medicine.

"A 13% year-on-year rise in 12-hour emergency department waits as winter approaches should set alarm bells ringing.

"More than 50,000 patients waited over 12 hours from the decision to admit to admission in September - 1,686 people every day.

"They represent vulnerable people who are waiting far too long for a bed and staff trying to deliver safe care in overcrowded emergency departments."

The government says the 18-week mark could still be achieved, saying it was investing in NHS buildings and equipment to make services more productive.

It also pointed to disruption to care that was caused by the strikes by resident doctors, a dispute which has now been settled.

But the strain that services are feeling in September, before winter has even really got going, will be a cause for concern among NHS leaders and their political bosses alike.

articles.title: Two killed after building partially collapses in Turkiye’s Istanbul
articles.summary: Eight survivors rescued from the rubble as fears of further collapse slow operations in Istanbul’s Maltepe district.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed after a seven-storey building in Turkiye’s Istanbul partially collapsed, officials said.

Emergency crews were trying to reach at least two people who were believed to be trapped, authorities said on Thursday.

The cause of the collapse was not immediately known, and an investigation was under way.

The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait.

Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while search teams rescued eight more people from the rubble.

The rescuers recovered two bodies and were trying to reach two people still believed to be inside, according to the Istanbul governor’s office.

Earlier, Istanbul Governor Davut Gul said rescuers had made contact with a 6-year-old trapped in the rubble. It was not immediately clear if the child was among those rescued.

He warned that the building was at risk of further collapse, hampering the rescue efforts. Nearby buildings were also evacuated for safety, the governor said.

Istanbul and other parts of Turkiye are undergoing an urban transformation programme that aims to replace old and earthquake-prone buildings with safer housing.

articles.title: From France to Italy, Belgium to Greece, student protests spread across Europe
articles.summary: Across Europe, a protest movement that began with French high-school students is increasingly finding echoes in neighbouring countries, as young people
articles.body: Across Europe, a protest movement that began with French high-school students is increasingly finding echoes in neighbouring countries, as young people complain about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, ageing school buildings, rising education costs and cuts to public spending.The unrest is not being organised as a single Europe-wide movement. The grievances are different from country to country, but the concerns are strikingly similar. Students are increasingly questioning whether governments are putting enough money into education at a time when schools and universities are struggling with staff shortages, infrastructure problems and higher costs.France becomes the flashpointThe movement began in the Paris region in mid-September, when high-school students and teachers protested over a lack of resources and staff. It quickly spread across France, with students blocking school entrances and later joined by university students, parents and trade unions.Their complaints include overcrowded classrooms, teachers not being replaced when absent, long school hours, deteriorating buildings and inequalities between schools in wealthier and poorer areas. Students have also raised concerns about the university admissions system and the pressure of the education system.The scale of the protests has grown considerably. More than 6,500 people have been arrested since the movement began, most of them minors, while hundreds of schools have been disrupted. The protests have also led to clashes with police and serious injuries.The issue of police conduct has become a major part of the debate after a 15-year-old boy lost his hand during a confrontation in Lens. The French government has since suspended the use of stun grenades in student protests and opened investigations into police conduct.The protests are also taking place against a difficult financial backdrop. The French government is under pressure to control its deficit while students and teachers are demanding greater investment in public education. The government has promised measures to address the concerns, but protesters say they want concrete changes rather than assurances.From Belgium to Italy and GreeceThe unrest has now crossed France's borders. In Belgium, hundreds of students took to the streets of Liège on Wednesday, citing rising education costs, overcrowded classrooms and limited access to study materials. The demonstrations have already resulted in arrests and clashes with police. The movement has echoes of protests in Brussels earlier this year over proposed education reforms, including an increase in tuition fees for students in Belgium's French-speaking community.Belgian students have also openly linked their protests to what is happening across the border in France, showing how quickly the French movement has become a reference point for young protesters elsewhere.In Italy, high-school students have begun occupying schools in Turin and Rome under the slogan "Let's do as in France." Their complaints include inadequate funding, deteriorating school buildings and the rising cost of living. Italian students have also travelled to Paris in solidarity with the French movement.Greece is also seeing mobilisation. Students have called nationwide school actions, including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and possible occupations. The immediate issues vary, but the broader demand is similar, with students seeking greater government investment in education.A wider European problemThe protests extend beyond schools themselves. In Ireland, thousands of university students have demonstrated in Dublin over tuition fees, higher-education funding and the cost of accommodation. In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions have demanded greater investment, more teachers and a fairer education system.Austria is facing another version of the same problem. Student groups are preparing demonstrations after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget.Taken together, the protests point to a wider European tension. Governments are trying to control deficits and manage higher borrowing costs, while students and education workers are demanding more spending on services they say have already been stretched too far.That does not mean Europe is witnessing one coordinated student uprising. Each country has its own education system, political circumstances and immediate grievances. But the French protests have provided a visible example for students elsewhere, while the underlying concerns are remarkably similar.For many young Europeans, the argument is increasingly about what they are being asked to accept in classrooms and universities today, and whether governments are willing to spend enough to improve the education system they will depend on tomorrow.You use AI every day. articles.title: VinFast eyes India e2W market, signs up 50+ dealers
articles.summary: VinFast plans India entry in electric two-wheelers, signing LOIs with 50+ dealers across 34 cities in 15 states, alongside charging and after-sales expansion.
articles.body: Chennai: Vietnamese electric vehicle maker VinFast is stepping up its India expansion beyond electric cars, preparing to enter the country’s fast-growing electric two-wheeler market with a network of more than 50 dealers across 34 cities in 15 states and Union territories.The company on Thursday signed Letters of Intent (LOIs) with its first 50-plus e-motorcycle dealer partners, marking the beginning of its dedicated electric two-wheeler distribution network in India.The move comes as VinFast is building its presence in the Indian electric vehicle market with manufacturing and assembly operations, including its planned manufacturing complex at Tuticorin in southern Tamil Nadu. The company had entered the Indian market in 2025 with electric cars and is now looking to tap the much larger two-wheeler market.The LOI signing ceremony was held at VinFast’s manufacturing complex in Hai Phong, Vietnam, during a visit by its prospective Indian dealer partners, according to a statement.The proposed network will span key markets including Delhi NCR, Rajasthan and Punjab in the north; Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh in central India; Maharashtra and Gujarat in the west; and Karnataka, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh in the south. West Bengal and Odisha will form part of its eastern network.The company said the cities have large two-wheeler markets and offer significant potential for electrification.“India is one of the most important markets in VinFast’s global growth story, and this partnership reflects the scale of ambition we hold for the region,” said Vo Thi Cam Tu, managing director, VinFast E-Scooters Overseas Market.Anurag Saxena, CEO, VinFast India E-Scooters, said the company would simultaneously work on charging infrastructure and after-sales services as it expands its dealer network. Partnering with dealers across marks the beginning of the company’s journey to bring VinFast e-motorcycles across India, he added.India remains the world’s largest two-wheeler market, with 21.41 million two-wheelers registered in FY26. Electric two-wheelers, however, accounted for only 6.54% of registrations, highlighting the headroom for further electrification.For VinFast, the move into electric two-wheelers gives it an opportunity to broaden its India portfolio beyond cars and tap into a segment where electric mobility has already gained significant traction.The company’s India strategy is also expected to be supported by its manufacturing footprint in Tamil Nadu, as it seeks to establish the country as an important market in its global electric mobility expansion.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: Up to 50 Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women
articles.summary: Chief constable Jo Farrell says more officers are likely to be suspended as officers are re-vetted.
articles.body:
The chief constable of Police Scotland has said up to 50 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

Jo Farrell said she expected more would face sanctions over their behaviour following a spate of former officers being convicted for sexual offences.

Farrell said a review into the handling of police officer Alan Greer – who was exposed as a serial rapist after taking his own life – was under way.

She added about 8,000 officers were still to be "re-vetted" for their roles after a change in regulations earlier this year.

A BBC disclosure investigation exposed Greer as a violent rapist who attacked and attempted to murder women over a 14-year period.

Further inquiries uncovered that Greer had passed vetting checks to join what was then Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record.

Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years

Police officer was violent rapist who attacked women over 14 years

Data published by Police Scotland via freedom of information request showed 63 members of staff were currently suspended due to ongoing criminal investigations.

Those include 45 constables, six sergeants and two inspectors, although the nature of each specific case is not known.

Farrell said that between 300 and 400 officers had now been revetted as part of new rules brought in following the murder of Sarah Everard by Met Police officer Wayne Couzens.

She said the rules would make it easier to "exit people" found to be unsuitable to serve in the force.

"It's only now during this year there has been a change in the vetting regime. So for the first time, if an officer fails their vetting, they can be exited from policing," she said.

"So that is a very recent change, and a welcome change from my point of view. Up until that point there were no opportunities to exit people from the organisation."

Farrell added: "My focus is on identifying where there is wrongdoing, criminality, particularly in relation to violence against women and girls and if that has been committed by our officers and our staff, that we identify it and we ensure that those people feel the full force of the law."

articles.title: Houthis claim new attack against airport in Saudi capital as witness reports evacuation
articles.summary: Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh on Thursday, including a large blast at the city’s international airport, a witness said, a day after the kingdom said an attack on the airport killed one person and wounded others.
articles.body: CAIRO — Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh on Thursday, including a large blast at the city’s international airport, a witness said, a day after the kingdom said an attack on the airport killed one person and wounded others. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen claimed the new attack on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, saying the ballistic missile caused damage but giving no evidence. The Saudis had no immediate comment about the claim. The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh, along with a ballistic missile fired toward Khamis Mushait, in the southwest near the Yemen border. The Houthis have repeatedly claimed attacks against Saudi airports, military and oil facilities in recent days. Early Thursday, the rebels warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which it called a theater for its military operations. The latest blasts had an immediate effect on markets and oil prices as the price of crude jumped. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh “closed again,” the Flightradar24 monitor said on X. “Last landing 80+ minutes ago. Last take off 90+ minutes ago.” Fire and ambulance crews had deployed and smoke was visible, the witness said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The witness said outgoing flights were halted and passengers were instructed to leave checked-in luggage behind and evacuate. It was not immediately clear how many flights were disrupted. Saudi aviation and other authorities did not respond to requests for comment. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said two attacks on airports claimed by the Houthis had killed three people, as the kingdom was pulled deeper into the latest front in the Iran war. They were the first deaths since Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces launched a major ground and air offensive aimed at retaking territory that the Houthis seized a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, and the attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 others, officials said. Attacks on the kingdom, the world’s top oil exporter, have raised alarm. The rebels’ presence on the Bab el-Mandeb poses a threat to the crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to the Iran war. The deadly attacks quickly brought condemnation from countries including Britain, India, the United Arab Emirates and others amid fears of an escalation. Also Wednesday, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said forces destroyed a platform in Yemen’s rebel-held capital of Sanaa that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital. The AP could not independently verify these claims.
